note: Only experiments that were actually run. Images live in creative-intelligence/experiments/<folder>/. Planned ones are in 'planned' and must not be cited as results.

experiments.question: Does the new inspect_views focal check agree with the earlier human judgement of the golden-glasses series (v1 lamp steals the eye, v5 fixed)?
experiments.controlled: same scene and intent; focal point given by hand at the glasses
experiments.method: inspect_views.py on tests/real/golden_v1-2, v4-1, v5 with --focal at the glasses
experiments.conclusion: All three measures rise in the same order as the earlier judgement; only v5 passes the focal check. Now a regression test in run_tests.py.
experiments.limits: 3 images from one series; the earlier judgement was Claude's plus the analyze_image read, not a panel of viewers. Saliency is a model, not eye-tracking.

experiments.question: With FLUX schnell, a fixed seed and a fixed prompt, does changing ONLY the light-direction phrase give a controlled lighting comparison?
experiments.variable: light phrase: side (raking from left) / top (straight down from above) / back (from behind toward camera)

observed: side: soft raking light and a long shadow, but the glasses' shadow falls to the left/back, not to the right as asked
top: the model turned the camera into a top-down flat-lay (the phrase 'from above' moved the CAMERA, not only the light); flat lighting; value span 0.30 (flagged flat)
back: no visible rim light; instead the glasses stand upright facing the camera, a gradient wall appears, temple tips turn black - product details changed
the frame's bridge and temple shape differ between all three

experiments.conclusion: No. In FLUX schnell a lighting phrase leaks into camera angle, composition and product design, so one-phrase variants with a fixed seed are NOT a controlled lighting test. Side/raking light gave the most readable product image here (only one seed).
lessons: Light-direction words like 'from above' can move the camera: say 'camera at eye level' again and describe the light by its effect on the surface
Text-to-image cannot hold a real product constant: product lighting tests must start from the real photo (compositing / relight) or a 3D/HTML render
For controlled visual A/B tests, change the variable outside the model (HTML/CSS layers, grading, crop) or fix geometry first
experiments.limits: one seed, one model (FLUX schnell 4 steps); not tested on Codex. Judgement by Claude from the images plus inspect_views numbers.

experiments.question: Can a post grade alone (no regeneration) move the eye from a bright lamp to the glasses? Which works better: desaturating or darkening the surround?
experiments.variable: grade outside a soft focal ellipse: none / desaturate 60% / darken 30% / both
experiments.controlled: same pixels, same focal ellipse, same mask fall-off; only the grade differs (fully controlled)
experiments.conclusion: Darkening the surround helped about 5x more than desaturating it (+0.24 vs +0.05). That fits the evidence that luminance contrast drives bottom-up saliency more than chroma does. No grade passed: a light source inside the frame stays the brightest spot. The real fix is composition (crop the lamp out or regenerate it off-frame), which is what v5 did.
lessons: Fix order for a stolen focal point: composition (crop/remove) > luminance (darken surround) > saturation
A grade cannot outweigh a visible light source; never leave a practical lamp brighter than the product
experiments.limits: one image; saliency model not eye-tracking; mask shape chosen by hand

experiments.question: Does FLUX schnell follow cartoon style words? Same subject, same seed, only the style phrase changes (8 styles).
experiments.variable: style phrase: chibi, modern TV cartoon, anime cel, 1930s rubber hose, crayon picture book, flat vector, b/w manga, webtoon
experiments.controlled: seed 777, 768x768, 4 steps, identical subject phrase (small round orange cat waving, full body, plain light background)

result.judged_by: Claude, looking at the sheet (no human rating yet)
followed_well: manga (b/w ink line; but no screentone)
partly: rubberhose (white gloves, noodle-ish limbs, grain/vignette - but stayed in colour though 'black and white' was asked; no pie-cut eyes)
flatvector (flatter shapes, still has thin outlines)
barely: anime (same cute sticker cat, no anime cel look)

experiments.conclusion: FLUX schnell has a strong default 'cute sticker cat' look for this subject. Style LABELS (anime, webtoon, chibi) barely move it; concrete rendering traits (black outline weight, crayon texture, b/w ink, white gloves) do. 'Black and white' was ignored once the subject says 'orange'.
lessons: Prompt cartoon styles by traits (line, shading steps, texture, palette, proportions with numbers e.g. 'head as big as the body'), not by style names
Remove colour words from the subject when asking for b/w
Label-only styles collapse into the model default; check a sweep before promising a style
experiments.limits: one seed, one subject, FLUX schnell 4 steps; judged by Claude only

experiments.question: Do trait-based prompts fix the 4 styles that failed by name in C1-001?
experiments.variable: prompt wording: style name (v1) vs concrete traits (v2)

result.rubberhose: fixed - grayscale, gloves, film grain (removing 'orange' + 'grayscale only, no color' worked)
result.chibi: partly - bigger glossy eyes, but head still not as big as the body
result.anime: partly - slender body, sharper line; artefact: one eye blank white
result.webtoon: partly - pink gradient background, glossy green eyes; character still the default cute cat

experiments.conclusion: Traits help: 1 of 4 fully fixed, 3 partly. FLUX schnell keeps its default cute-cat proportions; exact proportions (head = body) are not obeyed. For a precise cartoon style use a reference image (img2img / IP-Adapter, not installed) or draw the character in HTML/SVG.
lessons: Grayscale works only when no colour word is left in the prompt
FLUX schnell ignores numeric proportions; check eyes for artefacts in anime-like prompts

experiments.question: Turnaround in ONE image (sheet) vs 3 separate images: which gives correct views and a consistent character?
experiments.variable: S = one 1344x768 sheet / G = three 768x768 images (front, side, back)
experiments.controlled: same character text, seeds 101-103, FLUX schnell 4 steps

result.S_sheet: 1/3 correct (seed 101: front/side/back, outfit identical). 102: middle view is only a floating head. 103: front view drawn twice, no side view.
result.G_separate: 9/9 views correct; outfit consistent within a seed; seed 102 trousers light although 'dark' was asked; seed 102 has fake signature text
result.identity: within a sheet the outfit matches best; across separate images with the same seed it is close but not identical

experiments.conclusion: Separate generations with the same seed and the same character text were more reliable (9/9 views) than a sheet (1/3 usable). A sheet is worth trying only with several seeds, keeping the good one.
lessons: For turnarounds: same seed + same identity text, one view per image
Check for fake signatures/text in pencil styles (cv2.inpaint or re-roll)
experiments.limits: 3 seeds; Claude judgement; no similarity metric (DreamSim not installed)
